title: Dry-run: a MapReduce word count
intro: About 5 minutes. Word count is the canonical example because the whole model fits in ten lines — the interesting part is what happens between map and reduce.

steps.title: Map: one input record in, key-value pairs out
steps.explain: Each mapper runs independently on its own chunk of the input with no knowledge of any other mapper — that independence is what lets thousands of them run in parallel across a cluster.
steps.saysOutLoud: The mapper never needs to see the whole dataset, only its own slice.

steps.title: Shuffle: every key's values land on one reducer
steps.explain: Between map and reduce, the framework groups all pairs sharing a key onto the same reducer, hashing the key across the network from wherever each mapper ran. This is the expensive, all-to-all part of the job — most MapReduce tuning is actually about minimizing what crosses the shuffle.

steps.title: Reduce: one key, all its values, one output
steps.explain: By the time reduce runs, the hard part — grouping — is already done. The reducer just folds the list of values for its one key into a final answer, exactly like `Array.reduce`.

steps.title: Without a combiner, the shuffle carries every single pair
steps.explain: A mapper emitting one ['the', 1] per occurrence sends the word 'the' across the network thousands of times per document, when the mapper already had everything it needed to collapse those locally first.

steps.title: Fix: a combiner pre-reduces on the mapper's own node
steps.explain: The combiner runs the same logic as reduce, but locally on each mapper's output before shuffle — for word count it's literally the same function. This is a huge, nearly free win because it cuts network traffic without changing the final answer.
steps.saysOutLoud: The combiner is just running reduce early, once per mapper, before anything crosses the network.

steps.title: A straggler task holds up the whole job
steps.explain: The job isn't done until its slowest task finishes, and one bad node or one skewed partition (a single reducer stuck with a hugely popular key) can stall everything else that already completed. Speculative execution runs a duplicate of a suspiciously slow task elsewhere and takes whichever finishes first.

closing: If they ask why not just stream it instead: MapReduce fits a large batch you can afford to run once, on a schedule, tolerating minutes of latency — a stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams) is the answer once results need to update continuously as new data arrives.
